name: The Davisson-Germer Experiment
statement: Electrons fired at a nickel crystal diffracted like waves, confirming that matter itself has a wavelength.
statementAccent: confirming that matter itself has a wavelength
meaning: The Davisson-Germer experiment was a physics experiment carried out by Clinton Davisson and Lester Germer at what became Bell Labs in New York, culminating in 1927, which gave the first direct experimental confirmation that matter has wave-like properties. A beam of electrons was fired at a crystal of nickel, and the electrons scattered off the regularly spaced atoms of the crystal not uniformly but in a pattern of peaks at particular angles, exactly as waves do when they diffract off a regular grating. This diffraction of electrons showed that the electrons, ordinarily thought of as particles, were behaving as waves. The result confirmed the bold hypothesis put forward by Louis de Broglie in 1924 that all matter has an associated wavelength, given by his relation that the wavelength equals Planck's constant divided by the particle's momentum. The wavelength measured from the diffraction pattern matched the value de Broglie's formula predicted. The Davisson-Germer experiment thus demonstrated wave-particle duality for matter, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, and earned Davisson a share of the 1937 Nobel Prize in Physics alongside George Paget Thomson, who independently showed electron diffraction.
mechanism: The experiment works on the same principle as the diffraction of X-rays by crystals, but with electrons in place of light. A beam of low-energy electrons, accelerated through a modest voltage, was directed at the surface of a nickel crystal, and a movable detector measured the intensity of electrons scattered in different directions. Because the atoms in the crystal are arranged in a regular, repeating lattice, they act like a diffraction grating: waves scattering off the ordered rows of atoms interfere, reinforcing at certain angles and cancelling at others, producing peaks of scattered intensity at specific angles determined by the spacing of the atoms and the wavelength of the waves. Davisson and Germer found just such peaks in the scattered electrons, which is possible only if the electrons behave as waves with a definite wavelength. Applying the same condition used for X-ray diffraction, they calculated the electron wavelength from the angle of the peak and the known atomic spacing, and it agreed with the wavelength predicted by de Broglie's relation for electrons of that momentum. The crucial ordered crystal arose partly by accident, when air leaked into the apparatus and oxidized the nickel, and the strong heating used to clean it recrystallized the metal into a few large single crystals whose regular lattice made the diffraction sharp.

examples.text: Electrons scattered off the nickel crystal peaked in intensity at particular angles, the signature of wave diffraction off a regular lattice.
The electron wavelength read from the diffraction angle matched the value de Broglie's relation predicted from the electrons' momentum.
An air leak oxidized the nickel, and heating to clean it recrystallized the metal into large crystals that made the diffraction sharp.

whyItMatters: The Davisson-Germer experiment is a landmark of quantum physics because it provided the first direct experimental proof that matter has wave-like properties, confirming one of the most startling predictions of the emerging quantum theory. By showing that electrons diffract off a crystal exactly as waves do, it verified Louis de Broglie's 1924 hypothesis that every particle has an associated wavelength, establishing wave-particle duality not just for light but for matter itself, a foundational principle of quantum mechanics. This result helped cement the new quantum picture in which electrons and other particles are described by waves, underpinning the Schrödinger equation and the whole framework of atomic and subatomic physics. It also had far-reaching practical consequences: the wave nature of electrons is the basis of electron microscopy, which uses the very short wavelengths of fast electrons to image structures far smaller than light can resolve, and of electron and neutron diffraction techniques for studying the structure of matter. Davisson shared the 1937 Nobel Prize with George Paget Thomson for the discovery.

measure the scattered electrons and find peaks of intensity at particular angles, as waves diffracting off a grating.
compute the electron wavelength from the peak angle and find it agrees with de Broglie's prediction, confirming matter waves.

limits: The Davisson-Germer experiment confirms the wave nature of matter cleanly, but a few points deserve care. The definitive result came in 1927, though the underlying research ran for several years from about 1923, so 1927 is best described as the year of the confirming experiment and publication rather than the start. The measured and predicted wavelengths, around zero point one-six-five and zero point one-six-seven nanometres for the electrons used, are close but approximate figures from secondary summaries. The pivotal well-ordered nickel crystal arose partly by accident from an air leak and subsequent heating, so the discovery had a fortunate element. The 1937 Nobel Prize was shared by Davisson and George Paget Thomson, who demonstrated electron diffraction independently, but Lester Germer, Davisson's collaborator, was not included in the prize, a point sometimes confused.
misreadings: The Davisson-Germer experiment did not spring from a single year's work; the research ran for several years and culminated in 1927. The wave behavior it revealed is not confined to electrons in principle, since de Broglie's relation applies to all matter, electrons being simply light enough to diffract observably. And the sharp diffraction was not wholly by design, since the key ordered crystal formed partly by accident after an air leak, so treating the experiment as instantaneous, electron waves as a special exception, or the crucial crystal as fully planned, misreads the experiment that first confirmed matter waves.
origin: An experiment by Clinton Davisson and Lester Germer at Bell Labs, culminating in 1927, showing electrons diffract off a nickel crystal and confirming de Broglie's 1924 hypothesis of matter waves; it won Davisson a share of the 1937 Nobel Prize.
